What is GBrain?.topic: From Forgetful Chatbots to Persistent Brains
What is GBrain?.question: If RAG can retrieve any document in milliseconds, why does it still fail when an AI agent needs to track changes or maintain context across conversations?

options: Because RAG retrieves isolated snapshots but can't connect patterns or track changes across conversations over time.
Because RAG databases are too slow to handle relationship data at scale.
Because RAG requires a human to manually tag and categorize every document it stores.
Because RAG can only store text, not the metadata needed for relationship tracking.
secondary.answer: Because RAG retrieves isolated snapshots but can't connect patterns or track changes across conversations over time.

What is GBrain?.topic: The Two-Zone Architecture: Compiled Truth Meets Timeline
What is GBrain?.question: Why does GBrain separate Compiled Truth from the Timeline instead of appending all new facts to a single log?

options: Because combining both zones would require twice the storage and slow down queries significantly.
Because Compiled Truth holds your current synthesis that gets rewritten when updated, while the Timeline preserves raw events — mixing them makes current state ambiguous.
Because the Timeline is only used for debugging and should be kept separate from operational data.
Because regulatory compliance requires a strict audit trail that cannot be mixed with working knowledge.
secondary.answer: Because Compiled Truth holds your current synthesis that gets rewritten when updated, while the Timeline preserves raw events — mixing them makes current state ambiguous.

What is GBrain?.topic: BrainEngine: Storage That Doesn't Lock You In
What is GBrain?.question: What problem does BrainEngine solve that a direct database dependency cannot?

options: It automatically backs up your data to multiple cloud providers to prevent data loss.
It decouples the knowledge layer from any specific storage backend, so you can swap databases without rewriting application logic.
It compresses knowledge data to fit within the memory constraints of edge devices.
It provides encryption at rest, ensuring your brain data is always secure regardless of where it's stored.
secondary.answer: It decouples the knowledge layer from any specific storage backend, so you can swap databases without rewriting application logic.

Why Was GBrain Built This Way?.topic: The Iron Law: Content References Maintain the Graph
Why Was GBrain Built This Way?.question: Why does GBrain derive relationships from content references rather than asking developers to maintain a separate link table?

options: Because separate link tables require a dedicated database that increases infrastructure costs.
Because manual link maintenance creates a separate graph that drifts out of sync — content-derived links stay accurate automatically as content changes.
Because content references are faster to query than relational joins across a link table.
Because storing links in content makes it easier to export the knowledge base to other formats.
secondary.answer: Because manual link maintenance creates a separate graph that drifts out of sync — content-derived links stay accurate automatically as content changes.

Why Was GBrain Built This Way?.topic: Traceability: Every Claim Has a Receipt
Why Was GBrain Built This Way?.question: What does GBrain's 'every claim has a receipt' principle protect against that a simple knowledge base cannot?

options: It prevents unauthorized users from accessing sensitive data stored in the brain.
It prevents knowledge rot — you can trace which claims came from which source and update or invalidate them precisely when the source changes.
It prevents duplicate entries by checking if a claim already exists before storing it.
It prevents the brain from growing beyond a certain size by pruning unverified claims automatically.
secondary.answer: It prevents knowledge rot — you can trace which claims came from which source and update or invalidate them precisely when the source changes.

Why Was GBrain Built This Way?.topic: Sources and Federation: Brains Within Brains
Why Was GBrain Built This Way?.question: When would you choose to federate multiple GBrain sources rather than putting all knowledge into a single brain?

options: When you need to reduce storage costs by distributing knowledge across multiple cheaper databases.
When different domains need separate ownership, access controls, or update cycles but you still want unified queries across them.
When the total knowledge base exceeds a size limit that a single brain cannot handle.
When you want to run multiple GBrain versions simultaneously for A/B testing knowledge strategies.
secondary.answer: When different domains need separate ownership, access controls, or update cycles but you still want unified queries across them.

How Does GBrain Organize Knowledge?.topic: The Resolver: Automatic Filing for Entities
How Does GBrain Organize Knowledge?.question: What happens to knowledge quality over time without the resolver's automatic entity filing?

options: The brain runs out of storage because unstructured data takes more space than entity files.
Queries slow down because the brain must scan every file for mentions instead of querying entity indexes.
The same entity accumulates disconnected mentions across files, making unified lookup impossible without manual curation.
The brain rejects new content if it contains entities not pre-registered in a schema.
secondary.answer: The same entity accumulates disconnected mentions across files, making unified lookup impossible without manual curation.

How Does GBrain Organize Knowledge?.question: Why is a web of cross-referenced entities more useful than a flat collection of entity files?

options: Because cross-referenced files compress better and take up less storage than flat files.
Because real-world relationships are non-linear — cross-references let you traverse connections that flat files would require multiple separate queries to discover.
Because cross-referencing prevents duplicate entities by automatically detecting when the same name appears twice.
Because flat entity files cannot store relationships at all, only scalar properties like names and dates.
secondary.answer: Because real-world relationships are non-linear — cross-references let you traverse connections that flat files would require multiple separate queries to discover.

How Does GBrain Organize Knowledge?.question: What failure mode does the Brain-First Lookup pattern prevent that a purely reactive agent would constantly suffer?

options: It prevents the agent from making API calls that exceed rate limits by caching responses in the brain.
It prevents the agent from treating every request as starting from scratch, missing existing context and repeating work already done.
It prevents the agent from storing redundant information by checking for duplicates before writing.
It prevents the brain from growing too large by ensuring only query-verified knowledge gets stored.
secondary.answer: It prevents the agent from treating every request as starting from scratch, missing existing context and repeating work already done.

How Does GBrain Handle Data Flow?.question: Why does running entity detection and analysis synchronously create a worse user experience than async sub-agents, even if the total work done is identical?

options: Because synchronous operations use more memory, causing the agent to crash under load.
Because synchronous execution blocks the entire agent during each operation — async sub-agents keep the main flow responsive while parallel work happens in the background.
Because synchronous code is harder to debug when errors occur deep in the operation chain.
Because synchronous execution prevents the agent from storing intermediate results, causing data loss if a step fails.
secondary.answer: Because synchronous execution blocks the entire agent during each operation — async sub-agents keep the main flow responsive while parallel work happens in the background.

How Does GBrain Handle Data Flow?.topic: Cost-Optimized Model Selection: Sonnet for Detection, Opus for Reasoning
How Does GBrain Handle Data Flow?.question: Why is using your most powerful AI model for every task a mistake even when cost isn't a concern?

options: Because powerful models have strict rate limits that throttle your system during peak usage.
Because over-powered models introduce unnecessary latency on simple tasks — matching model capability to task complexity keeps the system fast and proportionate.
Because powerful models produce more verbose outputs that are harder to parse reliably.
Because using one model for everything creates a single point of failure that could take the entire system down.
secondary.answer: Because over-powered models introduce unnecessary latency on simple tasks — matching model capability to task complexity keeps the system fast and proportionate.

How Does GBrain Handle Data Flow?.question: What makes schema migration in a persistent knowledge system harder than in a conventional application database?

options: Because knowledge systems store more data than conventional databases, making migrations slower and riskier.
Because the timeline of past events must remain interpretable under the new schema — migrations must preserve historical meaning, not just restructure columns.
Because knowledge systems use graph structures that don't support the ALTER TABLE operations conventional migrations rely on.
Because knowledge migrations must run during off-peak hours to avoid conflicting with ongoing agent operations.
secondary.answer: Because the timeline of past events must remain interpretable under the new schema — migrations must preserve historical meaning, not just restructure columns.

Who Maintains the Brain?.question: Why can't you simply check for signals on-demand when a user query arrives, instead of running continuous watchers?

options: Because on-demand checks would require additional API calls that exceed rate limits during peak traffic.
Because by the time a query surfaces a stale signal, the damage is already done — continuous watchers catch problems before they corrupt output.
Because on-demand signal checking requires locking the database, making the system unavailable during checks.
Because users don't want to wait for signal validation to complete before receiving their results.
secondary.answer: Because by the time a query surfaces a stale signal, the damage is already done — continuous watchers catch problems before they corrupt output.

Who Maintains the Brain?.question: Why does GBrain treat all shell job submissions as potentially hostile rather than trusting submitted commands by default?

options: Because shell jobs are run on remote infrastructure where the submitter cannot be reliably authenticated.
Because one malformed command could delete data or expose secrets — default distrust catches even well-intentioned mistakes before they cause irreversible harm.
Because all shell commands must be logged for compliance, and validation ensures the log is complete.
Because untrusted commands run slower, so validation routes fast-path commands to optimized executors.
secondary.answer: Because one malformed command could delete data or expose secrets — default distrust catches even well-intentioned mistakes before they cause irreversible harm.

Who Maintains the Brain?.question: Why is checking the recipient's current local time more important than just storing their timezone offset?

options: Because local time determines the language and formatting preferences for notification content.
Because timezone offsets change with daylight saving time — 'what time is it for them right now' is the live question, not a static offset that may be stale.
Because storing timezone offsets requires additional database fields that slow down user profile queries.
Because GDPR regulations require systems to know the recipient's exact local time before sending automated communications.
secondary.answer: Because timezone offsets change with daylight saving time — 'what time is it for them right now' is the live question, not a static offset that may be stale.

When Should You Use GBrain?.question: What fundamental tradeoff does PGLite's zero-config approach make compared to a managed cloud database?

options: PGLite uses an older Postgres version to maintain WASM compatibility, sacrificing some modern SQL features.
PGLite trades horizontal scalability and managed backups for zero-setup portability — the database lives in a local file you control entirely.
PGLite limits query complexity to keep the WASM runtime fast, so advanced analytics require migrating to full Postgres.
PGLite stores data in memory only, making it unsuitable for any use where data persistence matters.
secondary.answer: PGLite trades horizontal scalability and managed backups for zero-setup portability — the database lives in a local file you control entirely.

When Should You Use GBrain?.topic: Daily Operations: Health Checks and Recovery
When Should You Use GBrain?.question: Why run health checks at the start of each day rather than only when something breaks?

options: Because health check results are cached and only valid for 24 hours before they expire.
Because broken-state detection during live operations is high-pressure and reactive — pre-operation checks catch misconfigurations while they're still cheap to fix.
Because daily health checks generate metrics required for SLA reporting and compliance documentation.
Because the brain accumulates inconsistencies overnight and must be cleaned before processing the day's new information.
secondary.answer: Because broken-state detection during live operations is high-pressure and reactive — pre-operation checks catch misconfigurations while they're still cheap to fix.

When Should You Use GBrain?.question: Why does describing an upgrade in terms of what users can now DO outperform a technically accurate changelog?

options: Because technical changelogs are harder to write accurately and often contain errors that erode trust.
Because users make adoption decisions based on workflow value, not code changes — benefit-focused messaging translates technical work into the user's language of gain.
Because regulators require benefit disclosures in plain language before users can accept new terms.
Because technical terms confuse support teams, and benefit-focused messaging reduces upgrade-related support tickets.
secondary.answer: Because users make adoption decisions based on workflow value, not code changes — benefit-focused messaging translates technical work into the user's language of gain.

And that's a wrap.question: After seeing GBrain's full architecture, what's the single design decision that makes everything else — federation, traceability, async flow — possible?

options: The decision to use Postgres as the underlying storage engine, which provides ACID guarantees for all knowledge operations.
The Two-Zone separation of Compiled Truth from Timeline, which gives every other system a stable, queryable foundation to build on.
The BrainEngine abstraction, which allows the entire stack to be swapped between storage backends without changing application logic.
The resolver's automatic entity filing, which ensures all knowledge is structured from the moment it enters the brain.
secondary.answer: The Two-Zone separation of Compiled Truth from Timeline, which gives every other system a stable, queryable foundation to build on.
